claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
The conventionally processed alloy has high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Limited tensile ductility in the baseline alloy is caused by microcracking at weak lamellar or colony interfaces.
Adding less than 1 at.% Nb during melting and casting can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
Nb will preferentially segregate to lamellar colony boundaries during solidification and subsequent heat treatment.
Nb enrichment at internal lamellar interfaces will increase boundary cohesive strength.
Increased boundary cohesive strength will reduce stress concentrations at internal interfaces.
Increased boundary cohesive strength will reduce microcrack nucleation at internal interfaces.
Preferential Nb segregation lowers lamellar colony-boundary interfacial energy.
Preferential Nb segregation enhances bonding at lamellar colony boundaries.
Enhanced interfacial bonding suppresses microcrack formation during tensile loading.
Nb retained in the matrix impedes dislocation motion.
The impedance of dislocation motion by matrix Nb produces solid-solution strengthening.
The Nb-modified alloy will have statistically significantly greater yield strength than the unmodified baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will have statistically significantly greater ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will have statistically significantly greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the unmodified baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will exhibit a lower density of microcracks than the unmodified baseline.
The intervention is applicable to eutectic high-entropy alloys with well-defined lamellar colony structures.
Excessive microalloying may destabilize the dual-phase microstructure or form brittle intermetallic phases.
